import re

# Heuristic only: scan each option's defining clause (definiens) for negation markers.
# This is a lexical check; it cannot settle the semantic question of which option is intended.
options = {
    "A": ("Wasteland", "the land uncultivated", [r"un\w+"]),
    "B": ("Emergency avoidance", "an act without criminal responsibility", [r"\bwithout\b"]),
    "C": ("non set", "does not reflect the object aggregate", [r"\bnot\b", r"\bnon\b"]),
    "D": ("Children born out of wedlock",
          "born to men and women who do not have a reasonable marriage relationship",
          [r"\bnot\b", r"\bout of\b"]),
}

neg = {}
for k, (concept, definiens, pats) in options.items():
    hits = [m.group(0) for p in pats for m in re.finditer(p, definiens, re.I)]
    neg[k] = hits
    print(k, "| concept:", concept, "| negation markers in definiens:", hits)

with_neg = [k for k, v in neg.items() if v]
print("Options whose definiens contains negation:", with_neg)

submitted = "C"
print("Submitted answer:", submitted)
print("Submitted option has negation marker:", bool(neg[submitted]))
print("Number of options with negation markers:", len(with_neg))

# The lexical scan shows A, B, C and D all contain negation. So it cannot single out C,
# and it cannot show that C is the unique correct option.
if len(with_neg) != 1:
    print("Scan does not isolate a unique option; the claim that C alone is correct is not verified.")
    print("UNSUPPORTED")
else:
    print("CHECK PASS" if with_neg[0] == submitted else "CHECK FAIL")
